items.stem: The project started in October.
Only experienced adults were allowed to join a mobile library.
The group received help from the village librarian.
The group solved its difficulty by buying expensive new equipment.
Nearly forty people became interested in the project.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Young Voices. Today we are speaking with Maha about a mobile library. When did the project begin?
Maha: It began in October, when people in a mountain village asked for something useful. Our group wanted everyone to take part, including students who had never volunteered before.
Interviewer: What was the first thing you did?
Maha: We started with arranging books by topic. We were supported by the village librarian, who showed us how to work safely and plan our time.
Interviewer: Was everything easy?
Maha: Not really. At one point, rain damaged some book covers. We listened to different suggestions before agreeing on using waterproof boxes. That helped us continue.
Interviewer: What was the most encouraging result?
Maha: I was happy when more families borrowed books. Nearly forty people became interested in what we were doing.
Interviewer: What is your advice to other students?
Maha: Start with a small idea. Ask questions, share responsibility and check whether your work is helping others. You do not need expensive equipment.
Interviewer: Thank you for sharing your experience.
Maha: Thank you. I hope more schools try similar projects next term.

sections.label: Reading 2
sections.passage:
When Maha heard about a mobile library in a mountain village, the idea sounded interesting but difficult. The project had started in October, and nobody was sure how many students would join. Maha decided to attend the first meeting anyway. At the beginning, the organisers explained why the project mattered to local people. They asked everyone to listen carefully before suggesting changes.

The group began by arranging books by topic. Maha was worried about making mistakes, but the village librarian explained that learning through practice was an important part of the experience. After a few days, everyone had a specific responsibility. Some students recorded information, while others spoke to families who visited the area.

A difficulty appeared when rain damaged some book covers. The group could have stopped, but the students discussed several possibilities and chose a practical solution: using waterproof boxes. They tested the idea, checked the results and made small changes where necessary. Instead of blaming anyone for the delay, they shared the work fairly.

At the end of the month, more families borrowed books. Maha felt proud and realised that a useful project does not need to be perfect on the first day. The students presented their work to the school council and suggested that another class could continue it next term. Maha kept a notebook with photographs and reflections, hoping it would encourage younger pupils to try something similar.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Young Voices. Today we are speaking with Salim about a vegetable garden. When did the project begin?
Salim: It began in September, when people in the school courtyard asked for something useful. Our group wanted everyone to take part, including students who had never volunteered before.
Interviewer: What was the first thing you did?
Salim: We started with planting seeds and checking soil. We were supported by his science teacher, who showed us how to work safely and plan our time.
Interviewer: Was everything easy?
Salim: Not really. At one point, the ground dried very quickly. We listened to different suggestions before agreeing on collecting rainwater in tanks. That helped us continue.
Interviewer: What was the most encouraging result?
Salim: I was happy when the first vegetables were shared. Nearly thirty people became interested in what we were doing.
Interviewer: What is your advice to other students?
Salim: Start with a small idea. Ask questions, share responsibility and check whether your work is helping others. You do not need expensive equipment.
Interviewer: Thank you for sharing your experience.
Salim: Thank you. I hope more schools try similar projects next term.

items.stem: Which weather is expected?
items.script: We wanted to organise a picnic near the coast tomorrow. I checked the weather report because it has been sunny for several days. The forecast now says there will be heavy rain in the afternoon. We will move the picnic indoors and choose another date.

items.stem: Where was the notebook left?
items.script: I searched everywhere for my history notebook this morning. It was not under my chair or on the teacher’s desk. Then I remembered using it in the library yesterday. The librarian found it on a high shelf and kept it safely for me.

items.stem: What will the visitors see?
items.script: My cousins are coming to Oman for the first time. They have already visited an airport museum and travelled on a traditional boat. Tomorrow we are taking them to an old castle, where a guide will explain how people lived there many years ago.

items.stem: The project started in November.

The group received help from her grandfather.
The group solved its difficulty by buying expensive new equipment.
Nearly fifty people became interested in the project.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Young Voices. Today we are speaking with Alya about a small local museum. When did the project begin?
Alya: It began in November, when people in an old neighbourhood asked for something useful. Our group wanted everyone to take part, including students who had never volunteered before.
Interviewer: What was the first thing you did?
Alya: We started with recording stories from older residents. We were supported by her grandfather, who showed us how to work safely and plan our time.
Interviewer: Was everything easy?
Alya: Not really. At one point, several labels were hard to read. We listened to different suggestions before agreeing on writing new labels in two languages. That helped us continue.
Interviewer: What was the most encouraging result?
Alya: I was happy when visitors understood more exhibits. Nearly fifty people became interested in what we were doing.
Interviewer: What is your advice to other students?
Alya: Start with a small idea. Ask questions, share responsibility and check whether your work is helping others. You do not need expensive equipment.
Interviewer: Thank you for sharing your experience.
Alya: Thank you. I hope more schools try similar projects next term.
